finding.claim: iconUrl is stored without any validation and later fetched server-side by the nightly sync job, allowing SSRF to arbitrary hosts (internal services, cloud metadata such as http://169.254.169.254/, localhost). The webhook URL is protected by a strict full-match regex, but iconUrl is not.
finding.source: The `icon` parameter of Profile.update(), supplied by the user via PUT /profile (src/Profile.java:11)
finding.sink: HttpClient.send with HttpRequest GET to URI.create(iconUrl) (src/Profile.java:23-24)

trace.note: update(webhook, icon) receives attacker-controlled icon from PUT /profile
this.iconUrl = icon, stored with no scheme, host or IP validation
sync() builds a GET request to URI.create(iconUrl) and sends it
Response body is read into a byte array. It is not returned in this file, so this is likely blind or semi-blind SSRF unless the bytes are exposed elsewhere.

finding.guards_checked: The regex check at line 12 applies only to `webhook`. `icon` has no check. No allowlist, no private-IP block, and no scheme restriction exist. The HttpClient is passed in as a parameter, and its configuration is not visible in this repo. Java's default redirect policy is NEVER, but that does not limit the initial target. The webhook sink at line 21 was checked and dropped: String.matches is a full match, the host is fixed to hooks.example.com, and the path is limited to 20 alphanumerics, so it is not exploitable (no userinfo, query or fragment can be injected).

verdict.reason: src/Profile.java:16 stores `icon` unvalidated (the regex at line 12 covers only `webhook`), and src/Profile.java:23 sends a GET to URI.create(iconUrl). Nothing else in the repo references iconUrl, so no other guard exists. The response is only read into a byte array at line 24, so the SSRF is blind or semi-blind.
